source.title: More findings on Memorization and double descent

record.tranche_reason: The post explicitly replicates a subset of prior toy-model double-descent findings, using a similar method with altered feature count, sparsity, and dataset-size range.
record.gate_note: The post reports qualitative double-descent results for dataset-size sweeps in toy networks. It does not report numeric curve values in the text. The final-layer section reports a second peak but does not state the sweep axis, so that result is recorded separately as bearing on no specific version. Other reconstruction, memorization, and geometry results do not measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The post sweeps training-set size in toy sparse-feature autoencoders (ReLU output bottleneck, two-layer MLP, cross-entropy unembedding). It reports a test-loss peak between memorization and generalization, which bears on V3. It replicates Anthropic's toy double-descent setup, not either original source's method, so it is a new setting (T3) rather than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The author concludes that double descent, i.e. moving from memorization to feature learning with more data, is consistent and predictable across the toy settings given sparsity and feature count. Test loss is much higher at the transition. Relevance to real transformers is uncertain.
record.recipe_differences: The post explicitly replicates prior toy-model findings but uses 1000 rather than 10000 features, sparsity 0.99 rather than 0.999, and a shorter dataset-size range; it also says it uses the original paper's schedulers.
record.method_sensitivity: The post says the schedulers make a difference. It also reports that bias initialization changes the superposition results, but does not connect that sensitivity to the double-descent curves.

fits_no_version.finding: In the ReLU output model, the double-descent transition occurs 10x earlier in dataset size with 10x fewer features. It falls at the same point across seeds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy sparse-feature models, the dataset size of the double-descent peak scales with the number of features and is seed-stable.

record.problems: The evidence concerns toy networks. Numeric curve values, uncertainty estimates, and explicit controls are not reported in the text. The exact location of the peak relative to fitting the training set is not stated.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant results were left out. Other reported sweeps concern reconstruction, sparsity, importance, noise, or memorization diagnostics rather than the tested claim versions.

untested.parts: Model-wise test-error curves as size grows. Hidden size is varied in heatmaps, but no model-wise peak is described.
Capacity-wise risk past interpolation across model classes.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting the peak.
Noise or regularization dependence of the peak, and multiple peaks.
Whether the peak coincides with the sample size at which training data are just fit; numeric peak heights.

missing.what: MLP heatmaps of test loss over hidden size × dataset size, described as double descent 'in all dimensions'. These could bear on a model-wise (V1-like) axis, but the text gives no model-wise description.
missing.locator: MLP block—Does it show double descent? (final paragraph)

missing.what: Seed consistency of the transition point.
missing.locator: Limits of reconstruction findings paragraph (bottleneck section)

record.verdict_notes: The record's T1 is wrong: the replicated work is Anthropic's toy double-descent paper, not an original source. All evidence is figure-based with no numbers, uncertainty, or controls. The rows' 'more data hurts' reading rests on the described loss peak, not on reported values.

versions.untested_parts: Model-wise test-error behavior as model size grows.
The exact alignment of the peak with the sample size at which training data are just fit, and numeric peak locations.
Capacity-wise risk curves across model classes past the interpolation point.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
Whether noise or variance drives the peak, whether peaks split, and whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
Whether an effective parameter count turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.
